prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Tesla, Inc." (ticker TSLA), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "TSLA", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Tesla, Inc.
result.industry: Electric vehicles, energy storage and AI/autonomy
markets: Driver-assistance and autonomous driving software (FSD) and robotaxi ride-hailing
Vehicle services, charging (Supercharger network) and insurance

mission.statement: Our mission is building a world of amazing abundance.
mission.source: Tesla Form 10-K for fiscal 2025 (Item 1, Business); adopted in early 2026, replacing "to accelerate the world's transition to sustainable energy"
mission.plain: Tesla wants to use electric cars, clean energy, self-driving AI and robots to make useful things and services plentiful and cheap for everyone.

about.plain: Tesla makes electric cars, like the Model Y and Model 3, and sells them all over the world. It also builds giant batteries that store electricity for homes and power companies. It writes software that helps its cars drive themselves, and it runs a self-driving taxi service in several US cities. It is also building a human-shaped robot called Optimus.
about.customers: Ordinary drivers buy its cars, homeowners buy its home batteries, and power companies buy its big Megapack batteries.
about.everyday: The Model Y has been one of the best-selling cars in the world, and Tesla Superchargers are the chargers many electric-car drivers use on road trips.

money.plain: Model Y, Model 3, Cybertruck and other electric cars, plus regulatory credits and leasing
Megapack grid batteries, Powerwall home batteries and solar
repairs, used cars, Supercharging, insurance and parts
monthly FSD subscriptions for drivers (about 1.48 million active in Q2 2026)
driverless taxi rides in Austin, Florida and other metros; Cybercab production started in 2026
a general-purpose robot meant to do factory and household work

result.summary: Tesla has a real but narrowing advantage: scale in EV manufacturing, its own Supercharger network, a strong brand, a leading energy-storage business and a large lead in real-world driving data for its camera-based self-driving software. But its core car business has lost share to cheaper Chinese rivals led by BYD, auto margins have fallen sharply since 2022, and much of its valuation rests on robotaxi and robot businesses that are not yet proven at scale.

pricingPower.evidence: Tesla cut prices repeatedly from 2023 to 2025 (Model Y in the US fell from about $66k in 2022 to under $45k, plus cheaper 'Standard' trims in late 2025) to defend volumes, yet deliveries still fell from 1.81M in 2023 to 1.79M in 2024 and about 1.64M in 2025; automotive gross margin fell from roughly 28% in 2022 to the mid-to-high teens. FSD pricing is firmer: the shift to a subscription model lifted active subscriptions 56% year over year to 1.48M in Q2 2026.

moats.evidence: Tesla is the best-known EV brand worldwide and spends almost nothing on traditional advertising, but surveys and European sales in 2025 showed the brand was damaged among some buyers by Elon Musk's politics (e.g. European registrations fell sharply in 2025).

Owners can switch to another car brand easily; the main lock-in is the Tesla app/software experience and FSD purchased for a specific car, and since 2025 most rivals in North America have adopted Tesla's NACS plug, reducing charging lock-in.

Millions of Tesla cars send driving data that train FSD, and more FSD users improve the software; the Supercharger network (over 70,000 connectors) grows with the fleet, though it is now opened to other brands.

Gigacasting, vertical integration and high-volume plants in Shanghai, Austin, Berlin and Fremont give low cost per vehicle versus Western automakers, but BYD's battery and supply-chain integration gives it an equal or lower cost base, with 4.6M NEVs sold in 2025 versus Tesla's 1.64M.
The car and battery-storage markets are large enough for many competitors; none is a natural monopoly.

Tesla's direct-to-consumer sales, over-the-air updates and camera-only autonomy approach are hard for dealer-based legacy automakers to copy without hurting existing businesses, though Chinese EV makers have copied much of it.

Manufacturing know-how (gigacasting, unboxed process for Cybercab), in-house AI chips (AI4/AI5) and an end-to-end neural-network driving stack trained on large data centers are hard to replicate quickly.
Tesla holds a large proprietary fleet-driving dataset and Elon Musk's ability to attract capital and talent, but it has no exclusive raw-material or regulatory asset.

customers.evidence: Tesla owners have historically shown high loyalty and satisfaction (Tesla led EV brand loyalty in S&P Global Mobility data in 2023-2024 and ranked near the top of Consumer Reports owner-satisfaction surveys), but loyalty slipped in 2025 amid brand controversy and US EV share fell to about 45% in 2025 from roughly half in 2024 (Cox Automotive).

talent.evidence: Tesla still attracts engineers who want to work on autonomy and robotics and pays heavily in stock, but it is known for very long hours, cut about 10% of staff in 2024, and has seen high-profile departures of senior AI, Optimus and sales executives in 2024-2026; it fell in engineering-student employer rankings such as Universum versus earlier years.

product.evidence: The Model Y and Model 3 remain strong on efficiency, software and charging access, and FSD v13/v14 is widely regarded as the most capable consumer driver-assistance system; but the lineup is old relative to rapidly refreshed Chinese rivals (BYD, Xiaomi YU7, Geely), and Waymo leads in fully driverless robotaxi scale.

competitors.note: Leading driverless robotaxi operator in US cities; main rival to Tesla Robotaxi

competitors.note: Mustang Mach-E and F-150 Lightning EVs; scaled back EV plans in 2025

threats: Cheaper, fast-improving Chinese EVs (BYD, Geely, Xiaomi, Leapmotor) taking share in China, Europe and emerging markets
Loss of the US $7,500 EV tax credit (ended September 30, 2025) and of regulatory-credit revenue as US emissions rules are loosened
Brand damage linked to Elon Musk's political activity, which hurt sales in Europe and among some US buyers
Waymo and Chinese robotaxi operators scaling driverless services faster, or safety incidents and regulation slowing Tesla's unsupervised FSD
Heavy capex on AI compute, Cybercab, Optimus and Semi pushing free cash flow negative in 2026 while auto margins are thin
Key-person risk and governance concerns around Elon Musk's attention, split across SpaceX/xAI and other companies
Tariffs raising battery and component costs, which cut energy gross margin to about 20% in Q2 2026

ceo.name: Elon Musk
ceo.background: Co-founder (early investor and chairman from 2004); BA in economics (Wharton) and BS in physics, University of Pennsylvania; founded Zip2, X.com/PayPal and SpaceX

c1.evidence: Tesla pioneered the modern EV industry and leads in US EV sales (about 45% share in 2025) and fleet-trained autonomy, but BYD overtook it as the world's largest BEV seller in 2025 (Tesla's global BEV share fell to about 11.9% from 16.5%).

c2.evidence: Buyers pick Tesla for software, efficiency, the Supercharger network, FSD and brand, but rivals have opened access to Superchargers via NACS and Chinese makers match features at lower prices, so the edge is eroding outside autonomy.

c3.evidence: Tesla is a household name and is still the default EV brand in the US; Model Y was the world's best-selling car in 2023 and remains among the top sellers, though recommend-rates dipped amid 2025 brand controversy.

c4.evidence: For almost 20 years Tesla stressed 'accelerating the world's transition to sustainable energy', then in 2026 replaced it with 'building a world of amazing abundance'; management is clearly purpose-driven but the 2025 CEO award worth up to about $1 trillion in stock raised questions about money motives.

c5.evidence: Millions of EV drivers, Supercharger users, utilities relying on Megapacks to stabilise grids (46.7 GWh deployed in 2025) and FSD subscribers would all miss Tesla, and it forced the whole car industry to go electric faster.

c6.evidence: “innovative, electric, Elon Musk, polarizing” – the product is mostly admired, but since 2024-2025 the public impression has become divided because of Musk's politics, so it is mixed rather than mostly positive.

c7.evidence: Tesla rides several secular trends at once: vehicle electrification (about 20.9M plug-in vehicles sold globally in 2025), grid battery storage, autonomous ride-hailing and humanoid robotics, each a market of hundreds of billions of dollars or more.

c8.evidence: Its AI, battery and manufacturing know-how let it expand into robotaxis (Cybercab production began in 2026), Optimus humanoid robots, the Semi truck (Nevada plant commissioning in 2026) and utility-scale energy.

m1.evidence: Musk has laid out multi-decade 'Master Plans' (2006, 2016, 2023, and Part IV in 2025) predicting EVs, solar-plus-storage, autonomy and humanoid robots long before they were mainstream.

m2.evidence: Musk has led Tesla since 2008, famously sleeps at factories during production crises, and in 2025 shareholders approved a pay plan tying his rewards to reaching an $8.5 trillion market value over about a decade.

m4.evidence: Musk is known for a demanding, top-down style (e.g. abrupt 2024 layoffs of over 10% of staff including the Supercharger team) rather than servant leadership.

m5.evidence: He built an engineering-first 'hardcore' culture that has repeatedly shipped new products such as gigacasting, the 4680 cell, Megapack, FSD's end-to-end neural net, Cybertruck, Cybercab and Optimus.

m6.evidence: Musk is personally involved in vehicle, AI and factory engineering decisions, holds physics training and serves as chief engineer at SpaceX.

m7.evidence: He has long framed his work around sustainable energy and making humanity multi-planetary, but his political activities, public conduct and huge pay package make his character contested.

m7b.evidence: Musk gave the 2012 commencement address at Caltech and the 2014 commencement speech at USC's Marshall School of Business.

m8b.evidence: Elon Musk is one of the most recognisable and outspoken business personalities in the world, very active on X, the platform he owns.

m9.evidence: He took Tesla from niche start-up to about 1.8M deliveries a year and built Megapack into a $12.8B business, but many promises (full self-driving by 2017-2020, $25k car, 20M cars by 2030) have slipped badly.

m10.evidence: Tesla is known for cost-cutting, minimal advertising and engineering out parts, but not for symbolic frugality, and it spends lavishly on AI compute.

c10.evidence: Tesla's cars and Megapacks cut emissions and make grids more reliable worldwide, but its products are mainly bought by better-off consumers and utilities rather than improving daily life for billions of people.

p2.evidence: Mass-producing EVs profitably, building grid-scale batteries and solving unsupervised self-driving and humanoid robotics are extremely hard engineering problems that matter for energy, safety and productivity.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose from $31.5B in 2020 to $97.7B in 2024 but fell in 2025 to $94.8B, and 2024 grew only about 1%.

f2.evidence: Gross margin peaked around 25.6% in 2022 and fell to about 18.0% in 2025, while operating margin dropped from 16.8% in 2022 to about 4.6% in 2025.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Tesla had about $43.5B in cash and short-term investments against only $9.3B of debt and finance leases, with $86.9B of shareholders' equity.

f4.evidence: Operating income fell from $13.7B in 2022 to $4.4B in 2025, and operating cash flow has been roughly flat at $13-15B a year since 2022 ($14.7B in 2022 and $14.7B in 2025).

v1.evidence: Tesla offers the best mix of software, efficiency and charging in the US, but in China and Europe buyers can get similar or better features for less from BYD, Xiaomi and others, so it is not clearly best everywhere.

v2.evidence: Tesla long ranked near the top of Universum's US engineering-student employer rankings, but its standing has weakened since 2023 alongside layoffs and an intense-hours reputation, and it is not on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For list.
